q: How do we know something is true?
quickAnswer: Indian philosophy developed a sophisticated theory of knowledge around pramanas, the valid means of knowing. Schools accept different lists: Charvaka only perception; Buddhists perception and inference; Sankhya and Yoga add testimony; Nyaya adds comparison; Mimamsa and Vedanta add postulation and non-perception. Debates concern whether scripture counts as independent knowledge, whether knowledge is self-validating, and how error arises.

perspectives.view: Nyaya accepts four pramanas — perception, inference, comparison and testimony — and developed a detailed logic of inference and debate.
The Charvaka materialists accepted only perception, arguing that inference cannot be guaranteed and so claims about unseen realities are unwarranted.
Buddhist epistemologists such as Dignaga and Dharmakirti accepted only perception and inference, treating testimony as a form of inference.
Sankhya accepts perception, inference and reliable testimony, and uses inference to establish realities not directly perceived, such as unmanifest nature.
Mimamsa holds that knowledge is intrinsically valid unless defeated, and that the Veda, being authorless, is a self-standing source of knowledge about dharma.
Jainism frames knowledge through many-sidedness: claims are qualified by standpoint (naya) and conditional assertion (syadvada).
